transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-20 15:00 UTC | Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park, Marco Diaz - Redwood; Priya Sharma, Ethan Cole, Marta Ruiz, Tom Hsu - Aurora Health

Summary (auto): Quick demo focused on structured output / JSON mode and function-calling. Discussed schema enforcement, guardrails, streaming partial results, and Dedicated vs Hosted for latency/cost. Agreed next steps: pricing, security docs, POC.

[00:00] Lena: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Lena with Redwood, i'm the AE on the account. with me is Marco, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Priya: Good, thanks. Busy week but excited, thanks for doing this, we wanted a deeper look at JSON mode and the function calling because we're building a clinical triage pipeline and need structured outputs.
[00:20] Marco: Awesome. quick agenda: we'll demo the API and Console, show structured output with schema enforcement, then function/tool calling for downstream systems, and finally touch on deployment options (hosted vs dedicated vs private).
[00:35] Tom: Sounds good. we'll be measuring latency and reliability more than raw quality; also security stuff, Marta will jump in on that.
[00:45] Marco: Great, i'll share my screen and start with the Console. bear with me, screen is up.
[01:10] Marco: (shows Console) This is the API playground; here i'm toggling JSON mode and uploading a JSON schema that defines the output object shape: patient_id string, urgency enum, recommended_action object with fields. I send a sample prompt: "Triage this patient note and return structured JSON according to schema."
[01:40] (audio glitch)
[01:45] Marco: you can see the model returns a structured JSON and the Console validates it against the schema; if the model deviates, the runtime can either coerce or reject the response depending on the guardrail policy.
[02:10] Ethan: Quick question — when you say "validate" is that strict validation server-side or just a client helper? we need absolute guarantees for downstream systems.
[02:22] Marco: Good question. validation happens in the serving layer: we run a schema validation step post-sampling and before returning to the client. if invalid, you can configure retries, forced re-sampling, or mapped error responses. it's not just client-side.
[02:38] Marta: And logs — does that validation result go into audit logs? we need to show invalid response events to auditors.
[02:45] Lena: Yes, audit logs record validation failures, sampled tokens, and the final payload that was sent. we can show retention options in the security whitepaper.
[03:00] Marco: Now switching to function-calling demo. We'll simulate a downstream EHR call: the model returns JSON plus a function call specification. the runtime can map that to a configured integration (http post to your EHR) or return a structured payload for your service to call.
[03:25] Marco: (typing) In this example the model decides to call "create_triage_event" with payload: {patient_id, urgency, notes}. you can see in the Console we also show a dry-run of the outbound call with headers masked.
[03:40] Priya: If the model hallucinates a patient id or a code, can you block that? we can't let fabricated identifiers hit production systems.
[03:50] Marco: Absolutely. we have guardrails: schema enforcement, allowlist/denylist for certain fields, and token-level filtering. plus you can enable an enrichment/validation hook — we can call back to your ID service to verify the patient exists before the EHR call goes out.
[04:10] Ethan: That hook is synchronous? i.e., we can fail the call if verification doesn't pass?
[04:15] Marco: yes, you can configure the policy to fail or to route to a human-in-the-loop queue.
[04:22] (brief crosstalk)
[04:40] Marco: Now i'll show streaming structured output. this is important because you might want partial results to appear in the UI while the model completes, but still maintain schema guarantees. We stream tokens but the runtime buffers and validates the assembled object before marking it 'complete' — partial fields can be emitted as safely validated chunks.
[05:10] Tom: Any impact on latency for streaming + validation?
[05:15] Marco: minimal; the validation step is lightweight JSON schema validation and our runtime is optimized — typical extra 10-30ms network round trip dependent. For high throughput we recommend Dedicated with pinned GPU pools.
[05:30] Priya: Let's talk numbers — what's the median latency for a 256 token response in Hosted vs Dedicated?
[05:38] Marco: On average for a comparable open model, Hosted is around 80-120ms per token at moderate load; Dedicated can get you consistent 40-60ms per token with steady 10-500 QPS depending on instance choice. we'll follow up with a TCO and latency spreadsheet tailored to your load profile.
[06:00] Ethan: Are you using KV cache and prefix caching? we have a lot of repeated context for similar notes.
[06:08] Marco: yes, prefix and KV cache are built-in; Optimize provides recommendations for cache settings and batching sizes to reduce token costs while hitting latency SLOs.
[06:20] Marta: On security: does Redwood support customer-managed KMS and on-prem key wrapping?
[06:26] Lena: Yes — for Private deployments you can use customer KMS/HSM. Hosted also supports customer-managed keys in many regions; we'll attach the KMS integration docs.
[06:38] Marta: And SSO / SAML? we need SCIM and RBAC.
[06:42] Lena: Supported — SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, and granular RBAC. we also have per-route access controls in the Console.
[06:52] (short pause)
[07:10] Marco: back to the demo — i'm going to intentionally provoke a schema failure: send a response missing 'urgency' field. you can see the runtime catches it, triggers a re-sample with adjusted temperature and deterministic sampling, and then returns a compliant object.
[07:36] Priya: How many retries do you recommend? we don't want to loop forever and increase cost.
[07:42] Marco: default is 2 retries with adjusted decoding params; you can set a max total token budget per request or fallback policies — e.g., return a sanitized partial object plus an audit flag.
[07:55] Tom: For the POC we'll want a mode that never calls the EHR — just returns the safe payload so our test harness can assert fields.
[08:03] Marco: Absolutely, you can configure a dry-run integration that logs the outbound call but doesn't perform it.
[08:12] (ambient noise, pausing)
[08:30] Marco: Now switching to the API example. i'll show the curl call for JSON mode: we pass schema, temperature=0.0, response_mode=json, function_call=automatic. the sample response is returned and validated.
[08:50] Ethan: Do you support streaming via websockets? we have a websocket-based UI.
[08:55] Marco: Yes. streaming over websockets or server-sent events is supported; the same validation and guardrails apply server-side.
[09:05] Priya: For audit and compliance we need full traceability from prompt -> model -> validation -> outbound call. is that all captured?
[09:12] Lena: Yes, every request can be traced with token-level metrics, validation flags, and the final payload. retention and redaction policies are configurable per account.
[09:25] Marta: Want to confirm: do you store PII by default? we prefer to not persist PHI in logs.
[09:30] Lena: By default logs are stored for X retention; you can enable no-log mode and use customer-managed keys, or route logs to your audit storage in Private deployments. we'll include options in the security doc.
[09:45] Ethan: Quick nit — what about function-calling determinism? we have automated rules that expect idempotent behavior for certain triggers.
[09:52] Marco: you can lock decoding to deterministic sampling (temperature=0, top_p fixed) and also use template-based function arguments to force canonical formats. Combine that with schema validation and mapping rules and you get deterministic outputs for the same input.
[10:10] (internal note: 10min mark, demonstration continues with sample prompts and mistakes)
[12:30] Marco: i want to show a failure mode: the model returns a valid JSON but with a slightly wrong enum value. we configure mapping rules to map legacy enum options and also expose a 'confidence' field. if confidence below threshold we route to human review.
[13:00] Priya: That's useful. can we also get per-field confidence?
[13:06] Marco: yes, we can surface per-field token-level confidence heuristics and a normalized score. it's not absolute but it helps triage.
[14:20] Tom: Another question: for on-prem/private, what's the deployment footprint? we have constrained GPUs in our colo.
[14:30] Marco: Private can be deployed into your VPC or on-prem. the on-prem package supports standard k8s clusters with NVIDIA GPUs; we provide recommended instance profiles and a resource calculator. for constrained environments we can suggest quantized model variants and lower batch sizes.
[14:55] Priya: Are there any regulatory templates you provide for healthcare?
[15:00] Lena: We have healthcare-facing security docs and templates for DPIAs and data-flow diagrams; we'll include those in the follow-up.
[15:15] (discussion about pilot timeline)
[16:00] Ethan: For the POC success criteria: we want <200ms median latency for the triage JSON, 95% schema compliance, and no outbound calls with unverified patient IDs.
[16:12] Lena: good, we'll capture that and confirm the benchmark plan.
[16:20] Marco: i'll run a small bench with your samples once you share them.
[16:30] Priya: Cost — any rough ballpark for Dedicated reserved capacity for our 10-20 QPS expected?
[16:38] Lena: we'll send a tailored TCO but roughly Dedicated reserved starts at X per month for the smallest pool; we'll detail committed usage tiers and burst options in the spreadsheet.
[16:50] Tom: And SLA?
[16:53] Lena: SLA available on Dedicated and Private. Hosted has best-effort SLAs for free tiers but enterprise SLAs are available with contract.
[17:10] (short pause)
[17:30] Marco: last demo note: function-calling + tools. you can map model function calls to internal microservices or to third-party tools; we show retries, circuit breakers, and masking for PII in tool payloads.
[18:00] Marta: Logging level controls? we may only want error-level logs in production.
[18:06] Lena: yep, per-route logging levels, and you can filter fields.
[18:20] (closing demo)
[18:45] Lena: Ok, quick recap and next steps: Lena to send pricing and SOC2 by 2026-03-22; Marco to prepare benchmark plan and POC config by 2026-03-24; Ethan to provide sample prompts and success criteria by 2026-03-23. we'll schedule a 30-min kickoff for the POC next week. any final questions?
[19:10] Priya: No, thank you — this was helpful. we'll review and circle back.
[19:20] Tom: Thanks, talk soon.
[19:25] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription quality: audio had a brief glitch 01:40-01:45, occasional label "Speaker 6" where attendee couldn't connect name mapping. The transcript includes paraphrase in a few technical explanations.
